methods: Read all curated satellite, rocket, star, debris, series, natural and story card copy and the computed-fact rules.
Compared all 4,084 individual Earth-orbit card identities and launch dates with Jonathan McDowell’s GCAT; corrected 18 dates and suppressed two disputed launch dates.
Queried SIMBAD for all 729 figure-star records; compared positions, spectral classes and parallaxes.
Computed IAU constellation membership for all 744 figure entries with Astropy’s Roman (1987) boundaries.
Corroborated suspect and rewritten claims using NASA, ESA, operator records, original papers and the existing expert references.
Ran the complete Node test suite and rendered 12 representative changed cards with the real card renderer.
limitations: This is a catalogue-wide content review, not a claim that every historical statement has been independently corroborated.
Fetching a source page successfully is an access check, not proof that every claim attributed to it was verified.
478 original source pages were unavailable to the audit fetch, predominantly Wikipedia HTTP 429 responses. No bulk retry of rate-limited pages was attempted.

Published stellar measurements differ between catalogues, especially for bright stars and multiple systems. High-uncertainty distances retained below are estimates, marked with ~ in the app; no automatic Gaia replacement was made on formal error alone.
Live orbital elements and apparent brightness remain estimates from the existing orbital catalogue/model, not direct measurements made by this game.
Two debris objects retain disputed US catalogue associations; the cards now explicitly describe the uncertainty and omit unverified launch dates.

card_copy_changes.name: The Sun

card_copy_changes.after: A middle-aged star with **1.3 million times Earth’s volume**. Never look straight at it: point the phone, catch it, and keep your eyes on the screen.

card_copy_changes.name: Moon

card_copy_changes.after: The Moon spins once per orbit, keeping **nearly the same face** toward Earth. A slight wobble lets us peek around its edges. It drifts about **3.8 cm** farther away each year.

card_copy_changes.name: Venus

card_copy_changes.after: One **rotation takes 243 Earth days**, longer than its 225-day year. It spins opposite to most planets and is the brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon.

card_copy_changes.after: Its rings are countless chunks of **ice and rock**, hidden around that steady golden dot until you use a telescope. Saturn’s **average density is lower than water’s**.

card_copy_changes.after: It spins almost **on its side**, with each pole facing years of sunlight and darkness. Under a truly dark sky, keen eyes can just pick it out as a **faint point of light**.

card_copy_changes.name: Neptune

card_copy_changes.after: The first planet found through **mathematical prediction**: Uranus’s unexpected motion pointed astronomers toward it in 1846. Too faint for unaided eyes; use binoculars or a telescope to find it.

card_copy_changes.name: Regulus

card_copy_changes.after: The heart of Leo sits close to the **ecliptic**, the Sun’s yearly path across our sky. The Moon sometimes passes in front of it, briefly hiding the star.

card_copy_changes.name: Polaris

card_copy_changes.after: The **North Star** lies close to the direction of Earth’s North Pole, so it barely shifts as the northern sky turns. It isn’t even among the **40 brightest stars** at night.

card_copy_changes.name: Hamal

card_copy_changes.after: Its name means **“the head of the ram”** in Arabic. It’s an orange giant about 66 light-years away, with a planet **more massive than Jupiter** circling it.

card_copy_changes.name: Tau Geminorum

card_copy_changes.after: An orange giant 30 times wider than the Sun, with a **brown dwarf** circling it every 305 days. Brown dwarfs lack the mass to sustain the **hydrogen fusion** that powers stars.

card_copy_changes.after: A **blue supergiant** in an eclipsing binary: its light dims slightly as a companion passes in front. Several other stars crowd around it in our sky.

card_copy_changes.after: A rare pair where one star has lost almost all its **hydrogen**. Gas transferred between the stars has changed how they evolve. They’re about 1,800 light-years away.

card_copy_changes.name: Anwa Farkadain

card_copy_changes.after: A yellow-white star about 97 light-years away and **coming closer**. Its surface races around at **85 km every second or more**.

card_copy_changes.after: The brightest star of the **Southern Pleiades** cluster. Its two stars orbit in just **2.2 days**. Past mass transfer may explain why the main star looks younger than its neighbours.

card_copy_changes.after: A hot star spinning at **325 km every second or more**, wrapped in glowing gas. It belongs to the **Southern Pleiades** star cluster.

card_copy_changes.name: Pi Centauri

card_copy_changes.after: The main star spins at **340 km per second or more** and **bulges 22% wider** at its middle than from pole to pole. It has a partner star.

card_copy_changes.name: Zeta Coronae Australis

card_copy_changes.after: A young blue-white star, only about **76 million years old**, spinning at **300 km per second or more**. It’s about 190 light-years away.

card_copy_changes.after: A system of **three stars and a brown dwarf**, an object too small to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers stars. Two of the stars take **772 years** to orbit each other.

card_copy_changes.after: The **nearest O-type star**, a scorching blue star **ploughing** through dust clouds and pushing up a glowing bow wave. It was likely flung away when a companion exploded.

card_copy_changes.name: Mu Piscis Austrini

card_copy_changes.name: The Wow! Signal

card_copy_changes.after: A strong, narrow-band radio signal whose origin remains **unexplained**. Astronomer **Jerry Ehman** circled it on the printout and wrote “**Wow!**”. It has never been reliably detected again.

card_copy_changes.name: Heart of Pluto

card_copy_changes.after: Nine years to reach Pluto, and it revealed a giant **heart-shaped region** with a vast plain of nitrogen ice on its western side. On board is some of the ashes of **Clyde Tombaugh**, who discovered Pluto.

card_copy_changes.name: The Arecibo Message
card_copy_changes.before: A picture made of **1,679 radio pulses**, beamed at the Hercules Cluster: numbers, DNA, a person, our planets and the telescope itself. It will take about **25,000 years** to get there.
card_copy_changes.after: A picture encoded in **1,679 bits**, beamed toward the Hercules Cluster: numbers, DNA, a person, our planets and the telescope. The radio waves take about **25,000 years** to cross that distance.

card_copy_changes.name: Sputnik’s Beep

card_copy_changes.after: The **first artificial satellite**: a shiny ball with four antennas, broadcasting “**beep, beep**”. Radio operators around the world tuned in. The space age had begun.
